correctness.rationale: Using Iannucci's exact semiperfectness obstruction, the forbidden equation is equivalent to the absence of \(up+vq\) in \([a-M+1,a]\) for \(0\le u,v\le M-1\). If \(q\le a\), the residues \((a-vq)\bmod p\), \(0\le v\le\lfloor a/q\rfloor\), are distinct and forced into the terminal interval of length \(x=p-M\), giving \(a<xq\) and hence \(2xy>M(M+1-x)\); splitting at \(x=M/2\) yields \(xy>M^2/4\). If \(q>a\), then \(y(x+1)>M^2\) and even \(x\ge2\) gives the stronger \(xy>2M^2/3\). The actual exact-integer verifier was inspected and its finite census through \(k=8\) is corroborative, not the infinite proof.

final_claim: If \(n=2^kpq\) is weird, with odd primes \(p<q\), \(M=2^{k+1}-1\), and abundance \(a=\sigma(n)-2n\), then \(M<a<3M^2/4+M\); equivalently \((p-M)(q-M)>M^2/4\).
limitations: The coefficient \(3/4\) is not claimed optimal and does not reach Iannucci's conjectured one-third-scale bound.
Only weird numbers of the form \(2^kpq\) are covered.
